prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Merck & Co., Inc." (ticker MRK), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "MRK", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Merck & Co., Inc.
markets: Other oncology medicines (Welireg, Lynparza and Lenvima alliances, antibody-drug conjugates)
Human vaccines (HPV, pneumococcal, pediatric, RSV antibody)
Cardiovascular and pulmonary medicines (Winrevair, Lipfendra, Ohtuvayre)
Diabetes, hospital acute care and HIV medicines

mission.statement: We use the power of leading-edge science to save and improve lives around the world
mission.source: Merck company website, Who we are (merck.com/company-overview)
mission.plain: Merck wants to use cutting-edge science to make medicines and vaccines that keep people alive and healthier everywhere.

about.plain: Merck invents and sells medicines and vaccines. Its biggest product, Keytruda, helps a person's own immune system attack cancer. It also makes vaccines like Gardasil, which protects against a virus that can cause cancer, and medicines for heart, lung and other illnesses. It has a separate business that makes medicines for farm animals and pets.
about.customers: Hospitals, doctors, pharmacies, governments and health insurers buy its medicines and vaccines, and farmers and vets buy its animal medicines.
about.everyday: Many teenagers get the Gardasil HPV vaccine from Merck, and its Keytruda drug is one of the best-known cancer treatments in the world.

money.plain: an infusion or injection that helps the immune system fight many cancers
diabetes, hospital, HIV and other cancer drugs, plus pneumococcal and child vaccines
medicines and vaccines for livestock and pets, like Bravecto flea and tick pills
a vaccine that prevents infections that can cause cervical and other cancers
a new injection for pulmonary arterial hypertension, launched 2024
the first oral PCSK9 pill to lower bad cholesterol, approved by the FDA in 2026

result.summary: Merck has a real but concentrated advantage: Keytruda is the world's best-selling medicine ($31,680M in FY2025, 48.7% of sales) and is protected by patents and a huge body of clinical-trial data across dozens of cancer uses. The advantage is time-limited because Keytruda's main US patent expires in 2028 and US price setting under the Inflation Reduction Act is expected from 2029, so the moat depends on Merck's ability to replace it through Keytruda Qlex, Winrevair, Lipfendra and acquisitions such as Verona, Cidara and Terns.

pricingPower.evidence: Keytruda sales grew from $25,011M (2023) to $31,680M (2025) on patent-protected pricing and new indications, but pricing power is fading: Gardasil sales fell from $8,583M in 2024 to $5,233M in 2025 as China demand collapsed, Januvia faces Medicare price setting, and Merck's 10-K says US Keytruda sales are expected to decline materially once government price setting takes effect around January 1, 2029.

moats.evidence: Patents on Keytruda (US compound patent to 2028, EU 2031, Japan 2032-2033) and Gardasil, plus approvals across dozens of cancer indications backed by large trials, give strong protected positions. Doctor trust in the Keytruda brand is very high, though consumer brand matters little in prescription drugs.

Keytruda is written into many oncology treatment guidelines and combination regimens (e.g. with Padcev in bladder cancer), so oncologists are slow to switch, but switching costs for patients and payers are lower once biosimilars arrive.
Medicines do not become more valuable as more patients use them, aside from accumulating real-world data.

With $65,011M of FY2025 sales and $15,789M of R&D spend, Merck can fund large global trials, manufacturing and sales forces that smaller rivals cannot match, though big-pharma peers have similar scale.
Vaccine manufacturing (Gardasil, pneumococcal vaccines) is complex and served by few makers, which limits entry somewhat, but most of Merck's markets have several capable competitors.
Merck uses the same business model as other large drugmakers.
Decades of experience running global oncology trial programs (Keytruda has the largest immuno-oncology clinical program) and making biologics and vaccines at scale are hard to replicate quickly.
Exclusive patent rights to pembrolizumab and to newer assets such as Winrevair (sotatercept, from the Acceleron deal) and Ohtuvayre (from Verona) act as cornered resources until they expire.

customers.evidence: Keytruda keeps growing (Q2 2026 Keytruda/Keytruda Qlex sales $8,366M, up 5% year over year) because oncologists keep using it across indications, but buyers are institutions and governments rather than loyal consumers, and Gardasil demand in China fell sharply in 2024-2025.

talent.evidence: Merck has a long research reputation and about 24,700 people in research activities at end-2025, but it is not a fixture at the top of broad employer rankings and has run repeated restructurings (restructuring costs $889M in FY2025).

product.evidence: Keytruda is the best-selling drug in the world and the leading PD-1 inhibitor by sales; Winrevair was a first-in-class pulmonary arterial hypertension treatment and Lipfendra the first approved oral PCSK9 inhibitor, though new PD-1/VEGF bispecifics such as ivonescimab challenge Keytruda in trials.

competitors.name: Bristol Myers Squibb
competitors.note: Opdivo and Opdualag compete directly with Keytruda in melanoma, lung and other cancers; also developing a PD-L1/VEGF bispecific with BioNTech.

competitors.name: Roche
competitors.note: Tecentriq competes with Keytruda in lung and other cancers; broad oncology portfolio.

competitors.name: AstraZeneca
competitors.note: Imfinzi competes with Keytruda; partner on Lynparza and Koselugo; rival in oncology broadly.

competitors.name: Summit Therapeutics / Akeso
competitors.note: Ivonescimab, a PD-1/VEGF bispecific, beat Keytruda head to head in a Chinese lung cancer trial and is a direct threat to its franchise.

competitors.name: Pfizer
competitors.note: Prevnar 20 competes with Capvaxive and Vaxneuvance in pneumococcal vaccines; oncology and hospital products.

competitors.name: GSK
competitors.note: Vaccines (adult and pediatric) and ViiV HIV medicines versus Merck's doravirine and islatravir programs.

competitors.name: Sanofi
competitors.note: Pediatric vaccines and Beyfortus RSV antibody versus Merck's Enflonsia (clesrovimab).

competitors.name: Johnson & Johnson
competitors.note: Opsumit and Uptravi in pulmonary arterial hypertension versus Winrevair; oncology (lung and bladder cancer).

competitors.name: Novartis
competitors.note: Leqvio cholesterol drug versus Lipfendra; oncology and cardiovascular medicines.

competitors.name: Amgen
competitors.note: Repatha PCSK9 injection versus Lipfendra; developing a pembrolizumab biosimilar for Keytruda's patent expiry.

competitors.name: Gilead Sciences
competitors.note: Biktarvy and lenacapavir lead HIV treatment and prevention, where Merck is building islatravir-based regimens.

competitors.name: Eli Lilly
competitors.note: Oncology (Verzenio, Jaypirca) and cardiometabolic medicines; competes for talent and deals.

competitors.name: Regeneron
competitors.note: Libtayo PD-1 inhibitor in skin and lung cancers.

competitors.name: Zoetis
competitors.note: Largest animal-health company; competes with Merck Animal Health in parasiticides (Simparica vs Bravecto), livestock vaccines and companion-animal drugs.

competitors.name: Elanco Animal Health
competitors.note: Companion-animal parasiticides (Credelio) and livestock products versus Merck Animal Health.

threats: Keytruda's US compound patent expires in 2028 (EU 2031) and Merck expects US Keytruda sales to decline materially once Medicare price setting applies from about January 2029; biosimilars from Amgen and others are in development.
PD-1/VEGF bispecific antibodies (Summit/Akeso's ivonescimab, BioNTech/BMS, Pfizer) could displace Keytruda as the backbone of cancer immunotherapy.
Gardasil sales fell from $8,583M (2024) to $5,233M (2025) on weak China demand, and vaccine policy shifts in the US add uncertainty.

Heavy acquisition spending to fill the gap (Verona Pharma ~$10B in 2025, Cidara with a $9.0B charge, Terns $6.8B in 2026) has pushed debt to $53,906M against $7,141M of cash and short-term investments at June 30, 2026, and may not earn its cost.
US drug-pricing pressure: Inflation Reduction Act negotiation (Januvia, later Keytruda) and most-favored-nation pricing proposals.
Clinical or commercial disappointment for replacement products such as Winrevair, Lipfendra, Capvaxive and Keytruda Qlex.

ceo.name: Robert M. Davis
ceo.background: Finance and law: bachelor's in finance from Miami University, JD from Northwestern Pritzker School of Law, MBA from Kellogg; previously Merck CFO (2014-2021), Baxter CFO and president of its medical products business, and about 14 years at Eli Lilly.

c1.evidence: Merck leads cancer immunotherapy, still a growing field, with Keytruda at $31,680M in 2025 sales, but the PD-1 market is maturing and Merck as a whole grew only 1.3% in 2025 (sales $65,011M vs $64,168M).

c2.evidence: Oncologists choose Keytruda because it has the most approved indications and trial data of any PD-1 drug, but that edge is protected mainly by patents that start expiring in 2028, so it is not durable for many years without replacements.

c3.evidence: Merck is a well-known century-old drug brand and Keytruda is the world's top-selling medicine, but most people know Keytruda and Gardasil better than they know Merck, and it is not a household default leader like Google or Amazon.

c4.evidence: Merck's stated purpose is to 'use the power of leading-edge science to save and improve lives around the world', backed by programs like its river-blindness Mectizan donation since 1987, though current management is focused on financial replacement of Keytruda revenue.

c6.evidence: “established, science-driven, Keytruda, Big Pharma” come to mind; the impression is mostly positive for its cancer drugs and vaccines, tempered by general distrust of drug pricing and the old Vioxx controversy.

c7.evidence: Merck's markets (oncology, vaccines, cardiometabolic drugs) are large and grow with ageing populations, but they are not a fast-growing secular trend like AI, and consensus expects revenue of only about $67.0B in 2026, up 3.1%.

c8.evidence: Merck is pushing into new areas such as oral PCSK9 cholesterol pills (Lipfendra), pulmonary hypertension (Winrevair), COPD (Ohtuvayre), long-acting flu antivirals (Cidara) and HIV, but these are extensions of a pharma model rather than a vast new market.

m1.evidence: Rob Davis has a clear plan to replace Keytruda revenue through business development (Verona, Cidara, Terns) and the subcutaneous Keytruda Qlex, but he is seen as a disciplined finance-trained operator rather than a visionary.

m2.evidence: Davis is a professional manager who joined Merck as CFO in 2014 and became CEO in July 2021; he is not a founder and does not own a founder-sized stake.

m4.evidence: There is no clear public evidence either way that Davis is a notably servant-style leader beyond standard corporate statements.

m5.evidence: Merck keeps a strong research culture (about 24,700 people in research, $15,789M of 2025 R&D spend), but under Davis much of the new pipeline has been bought rather than invented in-house.

m6.evidence: Davis trained in finance and law (Miami University finance degree, Northwestern JD, Kellogg MBA) and is not a scientist; research is led by Dean Li.

m7.evidence: Davis has continued Merck's access-to-medicine programs such as Merck for Mothers and the Mectizan donation, and there are no character scandals, but his public focus is mainly commercial execution.

m7b.evidence: No record was found of Davis giving a commencement speech at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university.

m8b.evidence: Davis keeps a low, conventional executive profile with no widely known distinctive persona.

m9.evidence: Under Davis sales rose from $48,704M (2021) to $65,011M (2025) and Keytruda kept beating estimates, but the Gardasil China collapse and costly acquisitions dragged 2026 non-GAAP EPS guidance down to $2.66-$2.76.

m10.evidence: Merck is not known for frugality; it runs periodic restructuring programs ($889M of restructuring costs in 2025) rather than a frugal culture.

c10.evidence: Keytruda treats patients across more than a dozen cancer types worldwide and Gardasil has been given to many millions of people to prevent HPV-related cancers.

p2.evidence: Discovering, testing and manufacturing biologic cancer drugs and vaccines takes billions of dollars and many years ($15,789M of R&D in 2025 alone) and directly saves lives.

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from 67.2% in FY2020 to 74.8% in FY2025, and operating margin (sales less cost of sales, SG&A, R&D and restructuring) rose from 12.0% to 32.6%, with a dip in 2023 from a large R&D acquisition charge.

f3.evidence: Equity is positive ($41,984M at June 30, 2026), but debt of $53,906M far exceeds $7,141M of cash and short-term investments after recent acquisitions, though it is about 3.3 times FY2025 operating cash flow of $16,472M.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from about $4,973M in FY2020 to $21,218M in FY2025 (calculated from reported line items), but operating cash flow was uneven: $14,109M (2021), $19,095M, $13,006M, $21,468M, then $16,472M (2025).

v1.evidence: Keytruda is the most widely used and broadly approved PD-1 cancer drug, a reason doctors pick it over Opdivo, but its main products are not clearly superior in a way ordinary people can see, and ivonescimab beat it in one trial.

v2.evidence: Merck appears in some employer lists such as Top Workplaces and has a respected science reputation, but it does not rank near the top of broad lists like Glassdoor's Best Places to Work.

c5.evidence: If Merck disappeared, cancer patients on Keytruda, families relying on Gardasil and other vaccines, and farmers and pet owners using its animal medicines would all miss important treatments.
